title: Every Type of WW2 Artillery Explained
fullText: Mortars. The story of World War II artillery begins not with giants, but with a weapon born for the mud, the mortar. This simple metal tube transformed infantry squads into miniature artillery batteries, delivering high explosives from behind crumbling walls. While heavy guns remained miles back, the mortar was the constant companion of the foot soldier, providing support when every second mattered. The American M2 2.36 in stands as a masterpiece. Weighing only 42 lb, yet hurling a 2.9lb shell over 2,000 yd. A disciplined crew could deploy in seconds, lobbing shells with a terrifying rhythm that bypassed the line of sight limitations of machine guns. Its extreme ballistic arc allowed it to strike enemies hiding in deep craters or behind 10-ft embankments with surgical precision. During the street fighting of Stalingrad, the mortar became the ultimate urban predator. Soldiers used these stove pipes to drop explosives vertically into enclosed courtyards over five-story ruins. A veteran crew could keep five shells in the air simultaneously, a lethal string of pearls impacting within a 3-second window. This created a hellscape so intense that survivors often believed a full battalion had struck them. By 1945, statistics revealed that the humble mortar caused over 50% of frontline casualties in some sectors. It proved that on a chaotic battlefield, striking from an invisible angle is more valuable than raw, clunky power. This steel type bridged the gap between the riflemen and heavy batteries, proving that the most sudden deaths often fall silently from the clouds. Mountain and pack guns. When heavy cannons were halted by jagged peaks or the narrow doors of transport planes, the pack gun stepped in to defy nature. These specialized weapons were designed with a radical modularity, allowing them to be stripped into several components for transport by mules or even human backs. While lightweight, they retained a savage power, delivering critical fire support for paratroopers and elite units operating in the world's most inaccessible theaters. The American M12.95 in pack howitzer stands as the gold standard of this versatile class. Comprising just six main sub assemblies, it could be fully disassembled in minutes, making it small enough to fit inside a C-47 cargo plane or be dropped by parachute in nine separate bundles. Despite weighing only 1,430 lb, a fraction of standard field guns, it could hurl a 13.2 lb shell over nearly 5.5 mi. This enabled light infantry to possess heavy teeth in jungles and mountains where traditional armor couldn't dream of venturing. In the brutal Italian campaign, these guns were often hoisted up near vertical cliffs using complex pulley systems to outflank German defenses. Their ability to be reassembled and firing within minutes of landing or reaching a summit provided a psychological shock to enemies who thought they were safe behind geographical barriers. It wasn't just a weapon. It was a feat of engineering that erased the enemy's high ground advantage. By the war's end, the pack gun had rewritten the rules of vertical warfare from the Alps to the Pacific Islands. It proved that firepower is only as good as its mobility, and no mountain was too high for a shell to reach. These compact howitzers ensured that even in the most remote corners of the globe, the reach of artillery remained absolute. Anti-tank guns. The anti-tank gun was engineered for a singular brutal purpose to shatter armored steel with flat trajectory precision. Unlike field howitzers at arch shells over obstacles, these specialized weapons utilize exceptionally long barrels to generate immense muzzle velocity, transforming projectiles into kinetic needles. They were the apex predators of the planes, designed to sit low to the ground and remain invisible under camouflage netting until an armored column wandered into a 550 hill zone. The German PAC 40 stands as a terrifying benchmark capable of propelling a 2.95 in armor-piercing shell at 2590 ft pers. This speed allowed it to punch through 5.2 in of vertical steel plate from 550 yd away, effectively neutralizing almost any Allied medium tank in a single hit. In contrast, the Soviet Z2 2.24 in focused on extreme velocity rather than shell size. Its barrel was so long that it fired rounds at a staggering 4,100 ft per second. This exterminator didn't rely on explosive filler, but on pure, terrifying speed to zip through the thickest Tiger tank armor like a hot knife through butter. In the vast Russian steps, anti-tank crews perfected the ambush doctrine, often holding their fire until the enemy was within 440 yards to guarantee a 100% hit rate. This forced tank commanders into a state of constant paranoia, knowing that any pile of rubble or dense hedro could hide a 6,600 lb weapon capable of instantaneous destruction. The psychological impact was as lethal as the physical one. It turned open fields into minefields of uncertainty. By 1945, these guns had grown into massive 3.46 46 in and 3.93 in giants, proving that no matter how thick the armor grew, a focused, high-speed strike could always find the heart of the machine. Field howitzers. The field howitzer was the indispensable engine of World War II, balancing brute destruction with immense tactical reach. Unlike direct fire guns, its lethality lay in indirect fire, using high angle trajectories to lob 33 pound shells over obstacles to strike hidden targets 7.5 m away. These weapons were the primary architects of the front line, shattering supply notes and providing the rolling barges that shielded infantry maneuvers. The American M2A1 105 mm stands as the gold standard, firing at a sustained rate of eight rounds per minute. Its split trail carriage allowed for a wide 45°ree traverse, meaning it could shift targets without repositioning the 4,980lb frame. Across the trenches, the German LEFH18 utilized a hydronneumatic recoil system, ensuring the barrel returned to its exact aim even after hours of bombardment. These machines allowed commanders to transition from bunker busting to area saturation in mere seconds. During the siege of Baston, howitzers achieved a mathematical miracle through time on target strikes, a technique where multiple batteries fired at staggered intervals, so every shell impacted the same coordinates simultaneously. This synchronized arrival meant enemy platoon were vaporized by a wall of steel before hearing the first whistle of incoming fire. By 1945, the field howitzer was the most statistically lethal weapon on Earth, proving that while tanks dominated headlines, Thundering Rain won the war. Anti-aircraft guns. The anti-aircraft gun was a masterpiece of high velocity engineering designed to snatch enemy bombers from the clouds using rapid fire mechanisms and vertical traverse capabilities. These weapons specialized in creating flat curtains, dense zones of splintering steel that forced pilots into evasive maneuvers. However, the true legend of these guns was born when they leveled their barrels at the horizon, transforming from defensive shields into the most terrifying direct fire weapons on the ground. The German 3.46 in Flak 18, famously known as the 88, is the undisputed Titan of this category. While it was built to hurl 20 lb shells to altitudes of 26,000 ft, its flat trajectory and massive kinetic energy made it an unintended tank killer. During the 1940 Battle of Heirs, when Allied heavy tanks seemed invincible against standard anti-tank guns, the 88 intervened, punching through 5 in of armor from over 2,000 yd away. It possessed a terrifying muzzle velocity of 2690 ft pers, ensuring that by the time a tank commander heard the report, his vehicle was already a burning wreck. On the Allied side, the 1.57 in Buffer's gun provided a different kind of lethality, capable of spitting out 120 rounds per minute to shred low-flying attackers. These weapons utilized sophisticated proximity fuses, tiny radar sets inside the shell that allowed them to explode near a target rather than requiring a direct hit. This technological leap increased the kill probability by nearly 300% late in the war. Whether defending the skies over London or sniping Soviet T-34s on the Eastern Front, these dualpurpose cannons proved that versatility was the ultimate weapon. Comment below which gun you think was more lethal at striking a target 5 miles in the sky and a heavy tank half a mile away with the same precision. Self-propelled artillery. To maintain the frantic pace of mechanized Blitz Creek, artillery had to shed its static nature and find its own wheels, or rather its own tracks. The self-propelled gun SPG was the solution. a hybrid beast that mounted heavy howitzers directly onto armored chassis. This innovation allowed batteries to shadow armored spearheads across cratered landscapes, ready to provide thunderous support instantly without the lethal delays of unhitching trailers or setting up recoil spades in open mud. The American M7 Priest stands as a prime example of this mobile evolution. Utilizing the reliable chassis of the M3 Lee tank to carry a 4.13 inch howitzer. Weighing approximately 50,000 pounds, it could cruise at 24 mph, ensuring that when the front lines shifted 10 mi in a single afternoon, the fire support was already there. Across the Rine, the German Wesa took a similar approach by mounting a 4.13 in gun on a light Panzer 2 frame. These vehicles were not designed for dueling tanks, but their open topped compartments allowed crews to handle a high volume of fire, hurling 33-lb shells at a range of nearly 6.5 m while remaining protected from small arms and shrapnel. The tactical genius of the SPG was the shoot and scoot capability. In an age where counterbatter radar was beginning to track incoming trajectories, being able to fire a three round volley and relocate 500 yards in under two minutes was the difference between life and death. During the rapid Allied breakout from Normandy, M7 units provided a continuous curtain of fire that kept pace with General Patton's sprinting third army, a feat impossible for traditional toad units. By the war's end, the SPG had transformed artillery from a slow, methodical rear guard asset into a lightning fast offensive weapon, proving that speed of movement is just as deadly as the weight of the shell. Assault guns and tank destroyers. Unlike traditional self-propelled batteries that fired from the safety of the rear, the assault gun and tank destroyer were frontline brawlers designed for direct confrontation. By eliminating the heavy, complex rotating turret, engineers could mount massive, high velocity cannons onto tank chassis that otherwise couldn't support such weight. This design trade-off allowed for significantly thicker frontal armor, creating lowprofile moving bunkers that were incredibly difficult to spot and even harder to destroy during a head-on engagement. The German StuOG 3 stands as the most produced armored fighting vehicle of the Reich, proving that a fixed superructure was ideal for defensive ambushes. Sitting just over 7 ft tall, it could hide in tall grass or rubble where a standard tank would be exposed. On the Eastern Front, the Soviet ISU 152 earned the terrifying nickname Zver Boy, or beast killer. This 100,000lb Titan carried a 6-in gun howitzer so powerful that even a non-penetrating hit from its 96lb shell could blow the turret clean off a German Tiger tank through pure explosive concussion. These vehicles functioned as the tip of the spear during urban breakthroughs and defensive standoffs. While the lack of a turret meant the entire vehicle had to turn to aim, their frontal protection, often exceeding 4 in of sloped steel, made them nearly invincible in narrow streets or long range duels. During the Battle of Kursk, these specialized killers proved their worth by sniping targets from over 2,000 yards away, effectively turning the tide against superior numbers. By 1945, the turretless assassin had redefined armored warfare, proving that sometimes the most effective way to lead an attack was with a low silhouette and a colossal fixed gun. Rocket artillery. If traditional artillery is a sniper's rifle, rocket artillery functions like a saw-off shotgun. These systems traded the precision of rifled barrels for total area saturation, capable of launching dozens of projectiles in under 10 seconds. While they lacked the surgical accuracy of a howitzer, they compensated by drowning entire grid squares in high explosives. A single truck mounted battery could neutralize a fortified village before a standard cannon could even reload its second round. The Soviet BM13, known as the Kushia, pioneered this mass destruction doctrine. Mounted on a truck chassis, it fired 16 rockets, each carrying a 4.1 in warhead in a rapid fire burst. This system delivered 5 tons of explosives over a 10acre zone at a range of 5.3 mi, leaving zero intervals for the enemy to seek cover between impacts. On the opposing side, the German six barrel Nevilleer used spinning stabilization to launch its payloads. This launcher could saturate a target with six 15 cm rockets in seconds, turning defensive positions into chaotic fire zones instantly. The technical advantage of rocket artillery was its shock and awe efficiency. The simultaneous arrival of multiple warheads created a localized over pressure wave so violent it could collapse lungs and shatter eard drums for soldiers inside bunkers. Because the launchers were lightweight compared to heavy steel cannons, they moved easily through deep mud and fired from forest edges before relocating. By 1945, the sight of rocket trails was enough to trigger a mass retreat. It proved that extreme volume of fire to be just as decisive as a direct hit from a heavy dun. Railway guns. Railway guns represented the absolute limit of landbased ballistics. Engineered on a scale so massive that no road could support their weight. These Titans required specialized multi-axxle rail carriages and dedicated tracks to move and absorb catastrophic firing recoil. Designed as strategic siege engines, they were built to pulverize formidable concrete fortresses from dozens of miles away. They stood as symbols of industrial ambition, transforming the railway network into a mobile platform for worlds shattering firepower. The German Schwer Gustav remains the largest rifled weapon ever used in combat, a 1,490 ton monster with a 31.5 in boar. It fired a concrete piercing shell weighing 15,700 lb, the weight of a full-grown elephant, at targets 23 mi away. During the siege of Sevastapole, one shell penetrated 100 ft of natural rock to destroy an underwater ammunition magazine. Operating this weapon required 250 soldiers for assembly and an entire anti-aircraft battalion for protection, making it a massive logistical odyssey. Despite their power, railway guns were hindered by reliance on fixed infrastructure and vulnerability to air attack. A standard 11in K5 could fire a 560lb shell over 40 m, yet required hours to calibrate on curved tracks. These guns existed where physics and engineering collided, demanding thousands of personnel to keep one barrel operational. By 1945, the era of the Iron Behemoth, faded, proving that while one shot could level a fortress, extreme complexity made them relics in mobile warfare. Naval guns, the pinnacle of World War II firepower, resided not on solid ground, but within the steel turrets of massive battleships. These naval guns represented the ultimate concentration of kinetic energy, functioning as floating fortresses that could dictate the fate of entire coastlines. When these leviathans closed in to support amphibious landings, they delivered a volume of destruction that made field artillery look like toys. A single broadside from a battleship carried more explosive weight than dozens of land-based batteries firing in unison, marking the absolute zenith of 20th century ballistics. The American 16in 50 caliber Mark 7 guns mounted on Iowa class battleships remain the most lethal naval rifles in history. Each barrel could hurl a 2700-lb armor-piercing shell, the weight of a midsize sedan over 23 mi with pinpoint accuracy. These projectiles traveled at 2500 ft per second, capable of punching through 30 ft of reinforced concrete or sinking an enemy vessel from beyond the horizon. Across the Pacific, the Japanese Yamato carried even larger 18.1 in monsters, firing shells weighing 3,200 lb. These weapons didn't just destroy targets, they altered the very geography of the battlefield, turning hills into craters and fortified bunkers into dust. During the D-Day landings at Normandy, naval gunfire provided the critical hammer that shattered the Atlantic wall. The shock waves from these 16-in blasts were so violent they could be felt miles inland, clearing paths through minefields and concrete obstacles that infantry couldn't bypass. The logistical scale was equally staggering. A single turret weighed more than a destroyer requiring complex hydraulics to manage the recoil of millions of footbs. Thanks for reading. Khán đài 36 in như một kiệt tác. Chỉ nặng 42 lb nhưng lại ném được 2. Vỏ 9lb nặng hơn 2.000 yd. Một phi hành đoàn có kỷ luật có thể triển khai trong vài giây, bắn đạn pháo với nhịp điệu đáng sợ bỏ qua giới hạn tầm nhìn của súng máy. Vòng cung đạn đạo cực mạnh của nó cho phép nó tấn công kẻ thù ẩn nấp trong các hố sâu hoặc đằng sau bờ kè 10 ft với độ chính xác phẫu thuật. Trong trận chiến trên đường phố Stalingrad, súng cối đã trở thành kẻ săn mồi thành thị tối thượng. Những người lính đã sử dụng những ống bếp này để thả thuốc nổ thẳng đứng vào những khoảng sân kín trên tòa nhà năm tầng tàn tích. Một phi hành đoàn kỳ cựu có thể giữ cùng lúc năm quả đạn pháo, một sợi dây chết người của ngọc trai tác động trong cửa sổ 3 giây. Điều này tạo ra một khung cảnh địa ngục khốc liệt đến nỗi những người sống sót thường tin rằng cả một tiểu đoàn đã có đã đánh họ. Đến năm 1945, số liệu thống kê cho thấy khẩu cối khiêm tốn đã gây ra hơn 50% thương vong ở tiền tuyến trong một số lĩnh vực. Nó chứng tỏ rằng trên chiến trường hỗn loạn, tấn công từ góc độ vô hình có giá trị hơn sức mạnh thô sơ, cồng kềnh. Loại thép này đã thu hẹp khoảng cách giữa súng trường và pin hạng nặng, chứng tỏ điều đó những cái chết bất ngờ nhất thường lặng lẽ từ trên mây rơi xuống. Súng núi và gói. Khi những khẩu pháo hạng nặng bị chặn lại bởi những đỉnh núi lởm chởm hay những cánh cửa vận chuyển chật hẹp máy bay, súng gói bước vào thách thức thiên nhiên. Những vũ khí chuyên dụng này được thiết kế theo mô-đun triệt để, cho phép chúng được tháo rời thành nhiều bộ phận để vận chuyển bằng la hoặc thậm chí bằng lưng người. Mặc dù nhẹ nhưng chúng vẫn giữ được sức mạnh khủng khiếp, hỗ trợ hỏa lực quan trọng cho lính dù và các đơn vị tinh nhuệ hoạt động tại những rạp chiếu phim khó tiếp cận nhất thế giới. M12 của Mỹ. 95 khẩu lựu pháo đóng gói được coi là tiêu chuẩn vàng của loại pháo đa năng này. Chỉ bao gồm sáu cụm phụ chính, nó có thể được tháo rời hoàn toàn trong vài phút, tạo thành nó đủ nhỏ để nhét vừa trong máy bay chở hàng C-47 hoặc bị rơi bởi dù thành chín bó riêng biệt. Trong chiến dịch tàn khốc của Ý, những khẩu súng này thường được treo lên gần những vách đá thẳng đứng sử dụng hệ thống ròng rọc phức tạp để đánh bại hàng phòng ngự của quân Đức.
